turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, the bus was hopeless, I know we're late. The chemist yesterday had my pressure at a hundred and fifty eight over 94 and I've been fretting on it ever since.
[SEG0002] person_2 (NURSE): You're fine. I've just done it here, 138 over 82, pulse 76. And the INR from this morning is 4.2.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, one second, the screen's frozen solid. 4.2, was it?
[SEG0004] person_2 (NURSE): 4.2, yes. This morning, before his tablet.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): That's why they told me to come in, they said the warfarin level might be high. 4.2, that's bad, isn't it? Am I going to bleed?
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): I feel like a wet rag as well. I've been so tired the last few days, I can hardly get going.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me pull the warfarin page up. You're on it for the atrial fibrillation, yes?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. The irregular heart. Five milligrams, every day. Well, mostly every day.
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He doesn't take the tablets on Sundays. I check the box. Sunday's still in the strip every week.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): No, no, that's not it. It's Saturday I miss, not Sunday. Bowls day, I forget. Sunday I have it with my tea, I always do.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Say that again? Saturday? This thing just beeped over you.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Saturday. Definitely Saturday. She had the wrong day.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Err, anything new prescribed? An antibiotic, something from another doctor?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): Out of hours, for this cough. Umm, klarithromycin, if I'm saying it right. 500 milligrams, twice a day, for a week.
[SEG0015] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Started Thursday, so four days he's had. And he's gone right off his greens. Spinach and cabbage, most days normally, now he won't look at them.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Greens. Sorry, say that once more, I'm half on this message.
[SEG0017] person_4 (CAREGIVER): The leafy ones. Hardly any since the antibiotic. They turn his stomach, he says.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): They do, yeah. And I've got a frog in my throat, catches whenever I talk. Is that the thin blood or the cough?
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding? Blood in the pee, black stools, nosebleeds?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. No nosebleeds.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bruises? Cuts that won't heal?
[SEG0022] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He nicked his shin on the gate. The cut healed in five days, ordinary healing, no oozing at all.
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): That's right, it closed up quick. I kept checking it. It was fine.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): If you lower the dose, though, am I going to have a stroke? My sister had a stroke, she was only seventy, and I cannot get it out of my head.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dose in a minute, I promise. Any chest pain?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Breathing's alright.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ankles swelling up?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really.
[SEG0031] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He sleeps badly, I'll tell you that. Up and down most nights for a fortnight.
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, that's fair. Awake at three, just lying there. Not every night, but most of them.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the sleep, how long did you say? I lost it.
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): About two weeks. Umm, I couldn't tell you the exact night it started.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): And my feet feel dead. Both of them. Is that the warfarin doing it? Do I need to be in hospital for the 4.2?
[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't put the feet down to the warfarin. Uh, one second, last note's just come up. You said the breathing was fine, but walking to the shops, any puffing?

[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I wasn't straight. I have to stop on the way to the shops, I'm puffing, I can't get a proper breath. Maybe I've overdone it. It's been there since the cough started.
[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the cough, how long?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Nearly a week. That's why I rang out of hours in the first place.
[SEG0040] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He coughs at night too. Sets the sleep off worse.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry, that tannoy, I can't hear myself think with it. Am I going into hospital or not?

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're not for hospital, there's no bleeding with that INR of 4.2. I think the level's up because of the clarithromycin and you've dropped the greens. Working impression only, not a bleed.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me just feel the pulse. Irregular, which we expect with the fibrillation. And the arms, no bruises I can see.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): So what happens to the dose? Do I stop the warfarin? Do I stop the antibiotic? Can I eat broccoli or will that shove it the other way?

[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): Don't stop the warfarin. Skip today and tomorrow, then 4 milligrams once a day instead of 5. Finish the antibiotic, only a few days left on it. Greens, back to your usual amount, the same each day, don't suddenly load them.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Four milligrams. What if I forget Saturday again? The match always overruns. I know I'll forget.

[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alarm on the phone, Saturday, same as every other day. If there's blood in the pee, black stools, a nosebleed that won't stop, or a big new bruise, go to A&E. Don't sit on it.
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): And if the 4.2 doesn't come down? Will you put the dose back? I'm sorry, I just keep thinking of my sister.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll see what the next INR says. I'm booking a repeat INR in a week, and I want you back here the same day so we look at it together.
[SEG0050] person_4 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him here. I'm in every weekday morning for the tablets. Saturdays he's on his own, that's how they get missed.
[SEG0051] person_1 (PATIENT): And the dead feet, and the throat, you're not doing tests for those today? I should have said the breathing earlier, I'm sorry.

[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the feet are still numb when you're back next week we'll have another look. The throat ought to ease as the cough does. I think that covers it, sorry I was glued to this screen.
[SEG0053] person_2 (NURSE): I'll send the INR request for one week today. Reception will text you the time. Mind how you go.

spec.situation: Older patient on warfarin for atrial fibrillation; INR result read aloud; antibiotic started elsewhere; green leafy diet changes; dose adjusted and recheck in a week.

traps.happens: A caregiver or relative reports observations ('the cut healed in five days', 'she sleeps badly', 'he does not take the tablets on Sundays'); the patient agrees, disagrees or corrects one point. The nurse also reports a measurement that the patient mentioned before.
traps.label_rule: reported_by follows who said it. A healing cut that healed normally is a negative finding (no slow-healing wounds) or nothing, NOT a symptom. A disputed fact is recorded with certainty disputed or as an uncertainty. A correction replaces the earlier value (Saturday, not Sunday).

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: INR result was 4.2 from this morning, before his tablet.
Patient reported a prior pharmacy blood pressure reading of 158/94 yesterday and had been worried about it.
Warfarin adherence detail was initially disputed: caregiver said he misses Sundays, but patient clarified it is Saturday he misses, definitely Saturday.
Clarithromycin had been started on Thursday and he had taken it for 4 days so far.
Leafy greens reduction was because they turn his stomach / nausea since starting the antibiotic.
No ankle swelling was elicited, though the response was equivocal ('sometimes, not really').
Initial denial of shortness of breath was corrected: he does get puffed walking to the shops and has to stop because he cannot get a proper breath.
Night cough was reported by caregiver and was said to worsen his sleep.
Patient asked whether he needed hospital admission for the INR of 4.2; doctor advised he was not for hospital because there was no bleeding with that INR.

Doctor advised that if foot numbness is still present at next week's review they will assess it further, and that no tests would be done for the feet or throat today; throat expected to improve as the cough settles.
Reception will text the appointment time for the INR/follow-up.
